_readme: Rules for scripts/scope-guard.mjs. They keep the v1.0 branch free of everything that belongs to the unreleased paid part, and they enforce the permanent store rules that stay true afterwards. The guard judges what is PUBLISHED: the file list comes from `git ls-files`, plus the built main.js when it exists, because the bundle is what actually ships. Run it with `npm run guard`.

_shape.rule: { id, why, kind: 'path'|'content', glob?: string|string[], pattern?: string, flags?: string, targets?: string[], allow?: [{ file, line?, match?, note }] }
_shape.path rules: match the repo-relative path against `glob` and/or `pattern`. They catch what no grep can see: a PNG of the trial screen, a committed .env, a wrangler.toml.
_shape.content rules: match `pattern` against the text of every scanned file, or only against the files matching `targets`. Binary files are skipped by content rules and covered by path rules instead.
_shape.allow: The pressure valve. A rule that produces a legitimate hit gets an allow entry with a reason instead of a weakened pattern - a guard that cries wolf gets switched off. `file` is a glob; `match` is an optional case-insensitive substring of the matched text OR of the line it sits on, which is how an exception is tied to the sentence that makes it legitimate instead of to a line number that shifts with the next edit; `line` pins an exact line number. `note` is mandatory: an exception without a reason is a config error.
_shape.self-exclusion: This rules file is never content-scanned; it would match its own patterns. It is still path-checked like every other tracked file.

rules.why: src/ai/ belongs to a later release. This one ships a search that runs entirely on the device and contacts no server, and a client for a remote service inside it contradicts both the README and the build.
src/license/ belongs to a later release. Entitlement code in a repository whose release gates nothing reads as a feature the description does not cover.
These view files belong to a later release and sit next to the ones this release does ship, which makes them the likeliest to be created here by accident.
backend/ is a separate deployable and belongs to a later release. It is not part of the plugin and must not travel with it.
A deployment configuration names infrastructure this release does not have, and .dev.vars is a local secrets file — the classic accidental commit.
The submitted repo has to be public, so a committed environment or secrets file is an immediate live-key leak, not a hygiene warning.
data.json is the plugin's own settings file from inside somebody's vault, and .obsidian/ is a vault configuration. Neither is source, and both carry whatever the machine they came from had in them.
This mockup shows an interface state that no released build can reach. It is a design file for a later release, and being an image it cannot be grepped — hence a path rule.
A privacy policy describing outbound data and LLM providers, in a release that sends nothing, is self-incriminating and inconsistent with the v1.0 README.
A second manifest published for testers advertises an unreleased build from inside the repository the directory reviews.
Tests are tracked files. A fixture for a service this release does not call describes that service as precisely as the client would.
node_modules must never be tracked; the build has to be reproducible from package-lock.json alone.

These are the names of provider credentials. Even as a placeholder or in a comment they imply the plugin is expected to authenticate somewhere, which this release never does — and a real one must never be committed at all.

allow.note: The guard's own end-to-end tests feed this rule a fixture repository, so they have to contain the literal name the rule looks for; a fixture that dodged the pattern would stop testing the rule. Scoped to this one file, so the name stays forbidden everywhere else in test/ as well. `test/guard.test.ts` asserts that the production rules report nothing against itself, which is what keeps this exception honest.

rules.why: No key of any provider ever exists in the plugin. In a public repo a leaked key is both a policy violation and a direct cost risk.
Route strings outlive the code that called them, in constants, tests, comments and translations, and each one names an endpoint this release does not talk to.
A provider or shop hostname in the source is read as an outbound connection by reviewers regardless of whether any code calls it.
A checkout or billing address anywhere in the shipped files points at something this release does not have, and asks for a disclosure it has nothing to fill in.

v1.0 is 100 % local. Zero network calls is the strongest claim the README can make and it makes the network-use disclosure moot. Any hit is either an AI leftover or telemetry. The built main.js is scanned too, because a flagged-off branch still ends up in the bundle.
Client-side telemetry is an automatic rejection and the second thing besides the AI part that the review bot pattern-matches on.

allow.note: @opentelemetry/api is an OPTIONAL peer dependency of vitest (peerDependenciesMeta marks it optional). npm records it in the lockfile without installing it, so it is metadata about a test runner, not code that ships. An actually installed telemetry package would also appear in package.json and is caught there.

rules.why: No logging of search terms or note content, not even locally: in an unminified bundle a debug log in the searcher is indistinguishable from telemetry. console.error in a genuine error path is the only exception and is recorded here as an allow entry.
innerHTML, document.write, eval and the Function constructor are blocker-level findings in the plugin review and are the rules that may not even be disabled inline.
isDesktopOnly is false, so a single Node or Electron import makes the manifest a lie and breaks the plugin on iOS and Android.
Only Obsidian CSS variables may decide colour; a literal colour breaks every theme that is not the one it was written against.
A default hotkey collides with the user's own bindings and with core commands; the guideline is to register none.
devDependencies are read too. A deployment tool or an HTTP client there implies infrastructure and network use that this release does not have.
A deploy script or a workspace entry names infrastructure that must not exist on this branch, and it survives long after backend/ was deleted.
Vocabulary outlives the code it described. A view gets deleted and the words stay behind in a comment, a class name or a translation key, where they read as a feature the description does not cover.

allow.note: The MIT licence text itself. A LICENSE file at repo root is required by the developer policies.
The npm `license: MIT` field, which must match the LICENSE file.
npm records the licence of every dependency in the lockfile.
The README's licence section (MIT), required by the submission checklist.
The fixture vault generator writes German and English prose as note content; a word like 'Trial' there is vault text, not plugin code.

Several test files run this same policy scan from inside vitest and therefore carry the forbidden vocabulary as test data. Tests are not part of the release. The sharp rules - backend routes, provider hosts, key material, paid file names - still apply to test/ unchanged.

A line that DENIES the paid part ('Phase 1 scope: local search only. No AI, no license, no backend, no network.' in src/types.ts) is a scope statement. A reviewer reading the unminified bundle sees the same sentence and it reads correctly.

rules.why: A mention of a language model anywhere in the shipped files, in either language, describes behaviour this release does not have and asks for a network disclosure it does not need.

allow.note: Several test files run this same policy scan from inside vitest and therefore carry the forbidden vocabulary as test data. Tests are not part of the release, and the sharp rules still apply to test/ unchanged.

A line that DENIES the AI part ('Phase 1 scope: local search only. No AI, no license, no backend, no network.' in src/types.ts) is a scope statement, not an announcement, and reads correctly in the shipped bundle too.

rules.why: CSS ships verbatim and is never tree-shaken. A .sift-upgrade rule with no markup behind it is a pure giveaway.

allow.note: `.sift-chip` is the filter bar's own chip - folder, date range and sort - and is Phase-1 UI straight from the mockup. The AI section's related-term chips carried the additional class prefix (.sift-ai-chip, .sift-related-chip), which this rule still catches.

rules.why: A single leftover field in DEFAULT_SETTINGS ends up in every user's data.json and in the settings tab.
Commands show up in the command palette and in the reviewer's manual test, independent of whether the code path is reachable.
A flag makes the AI code look harmless to its author while it still sits in the repo and in the bundle. A disabled feature is a shipped feature for the reviewer.
The store requires an unminified build, so comments ship. A note about work planned for a later release therefore becomes a public roadmap inside the shipped file.
The most likely leftover of all: the UI code is deleted, the translation keys stay. They are plain JSON, get inlined into main.js, and read as a feature list.
These README sections belong to the release that actually ships what they disclose. Here they would describe behaviour the build does not have.

allow.note: The v1.0 README's own section DENIES network use: no requests, no telemetry, no data leaving the device, index in IndexedDB. That is the disclosure a reviewer wants to find, the opposite of the v1.1 section this rule guards against. If the section ever starts DESCRIBING outbound data, remove this entry - the rule then applies again.

rules.why: The sparkle icon is the only AI-specific asset and travels with a copy-paste of the section header even when the text around it is changed.
Commercial text anywhere in the repository asks for a disclosure this release has nothing to disclose, and invites a question the build cannot answer.
Obfuscation is a hard rejection and minification without a sourcemap is treated as obfuscation. The build must stay readable.

'Obsidian' or 'plugin' in the id or name is a hard rejection; isDesktopOnly true contradicts the mobile target; an AI word in the description is the store listing text advertising an undisclosed feature.
fundingUrl is for donations only. A shop or checkout link there is a documented rejection reason.
A planning document for later releases is not part of what this one ships, and the directory reviews the whole repository rather than the release. It belongs wherever the rest of that planning lives.
These files sit at the repository root and are among the first anyone opens. A sentence there about work outside this release does the same damage as the code would.

The dark and light mockups stay on this branch as the Phase-1 UI target, so the AI block inside them has to be cut out rather than the file removed - otherwise the target picture invites building the AI section straight into the Phase-1 overlay.
